title: Kids outlearn AI—and we still don’t know why
gist: LLMs need roughly 100,000 times more language data than a child does to reach fluency, and with easily available internet text possibly exhausted as early as the 2030s, a small research community organized around the BabyLM competition is reverse-engineering child learning to close that data efficiency gap. Early results are counterintuitive: the best 100-million-word model beat Llama 2 70B on a benchmark, while the baby-inspired tricks — curriculum learning, video grounding, social interaction — have so far underperformed.

insights.claim: A large language model can consume roughly a hundred thousand times more words than a human needs to master their native tongue, making data efficiency — not capability — the sharpest remaining gap between models and children.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: Frames the core scaling risk: if capability keeps costing exponential data, the marginal return on further pretraining spend deteriorates.
insights.quote: An LLM can easily churn through a hundred thousand times more words than a person will experience in the process of mastering their mother tongue
insights.locator: But peek behind the computational curtain

insights.claim: Meta's Llama 3.1 chewed through 15 trillion tokens in pretraining two years ago, and frontier models could now be pretraining on ten times that amount, according to Georgetown cognitive scientist Ethan Gotlieb Wilcox.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: A concrete anchor for frontier pretraining scale — useful for sizing compute and data-licensing budgets against public disclosures.
insights.quote: chewed through 15 trillion tokens (word-like chunks of language) in pretraining
insights.locator: For the past decade, language models have mostly gotten better

insights.claim: The supply of easily available internet training data could run dry as early as the 2030s, putting a hard ceiling on the strategy of improving models by making them bigger.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: A dated exhaustion horizon: data-licensing deals, synthetic data, and efficiency research all get repriced as that date approaches.
insights.quote: eventually—perhaps as early as the 2030s—the well of easily available data could run dry
insights.locator: But there’s only so much internet to train on

insights.claim: A preteen raised in a linguistically rich home has heard roughly 100 million words, rising to perhaps 300 million by age 20 once literacy is added — the human benchmark any data-efficient model must beat.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: Sets the target order of magnitude; a model matching human fluency at 10^8 words would collapse pretraining cost by orders of magnitude.
insights.quote: A preteen raised in a linguistically rich home may have heard something in the vicinity of 100 million words.
insights.locator: Kids show that it could be possible to learn more with less

insights.claim: Toddlers begin producing grammatically correct sentences after roughly 10 million words of exposure — 30 million at the high end — whereas GPT-2 trained on 30 million words produces only nonsense.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: The cleanest single illustration that current architectures are not merely behind on data but qualitatively different learners.
insights.quote: If you train GPT-2 on 30 million words, you get a nonsense generator; you don’t get a kid.
insights.locator: It’s just totally miraculous

insights.claim: Stanford cognitive scientist Michael C. Frank frames current AI progress as environmentally and epistemically brute-force: recreating in a data center what a household achieves in a year requires consuming the sum of human knowledge.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: The efficiency critique is becoming the respectable scientific framing of the AI energy and data debate — expect it in policy arguments.
insights.quote: But we still have to burn down a forest and scrape the entire sum of all human knowledge to re-create this milestone that happens in our living rooms over the course of a year.
insights.locator: The progress recently has been amazing

insights.claim: Wilcox's scale analogy — that a frontier model has absorbed the language an entire city experiences in one generation, versus a printed stack 20 meters high for a preteen — makes the gap intuitive enough to travel in policy and investor conversations.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: Memorable framings drive narrative; this one arms critics of pure scaling with a vivid, quotable comparison.
insights.quote: Claude has seen the amount of language that an entire city will experience in one generation,
insights.locator: The difference in scale is something that can only really be gestured at in analogy

insights.claim: US AI research spent decades hand-coding grammatical rules into programs under the influence of Chomsky's generative grammar, an approach that largely failed to handle human language at scale and helped trigger the 1970s AI winter.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: A precedent worth holding: a dominant theoretical paradigm can misdirect an entire field's engineering agenda for decades.
insights.quote: This approach, part of a broader trend called symbolic AI, prevailed for decades. It also largely failed to produce models actually capable of handling human language at scale.
insights.locator: Despite early successes of simple neural networks

insights.claim: Chomsky's poverty-of-the-stimulus argument held that language cannot be learned from statistics alone, and LLMs are precisely the kind of naive statistical learner that generative linguists believed could never acquire syntax — yet they did.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: A live example of an empirical result overturning expert consensus; useful calibration when experts declare a capability impossible.
insights.quote: His signature argument was, essentially, that language cannot be learned on the basis purely of statistics,
insights.locator: Chomsky countered by citing the “poverty of the stimulus”

insights.claim: Berkeley developmental psychologist Alison Gopnik concedes that the syntax-learning ability of LLMs surprised even skeptics, and that most researchers did not expect grammar to fall out of statistics over a large sample.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: When a field's leading skeptics update publicly, the direction of subsequent research funding usually follows.
insights.quote: No matter how skeptical you are about AI, the thing that everyone has been really impressed with is: These things learn syntax,
insights.locator: LLMs are not brains

insights.claim: The transformer architecture plus billions of tokens made large-scale statistical language learning credible to insiders with BERT and GPT-2 in 2018–2019, three to four years before ChatGPT made it obvious to the public.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: The insider-to-public lag on architectural breakthroughs ran roughly three years — a rough calibration for spotting the next one early.
insights.quote: By 2018 and 2019, the models BERT and GPT-2, which were built on a new architecture—the transformer—and trained on billions of tokens, made it clear to insiders that learning from a massive glut of data could work for language.
insights.locator: In the aftermath, neural networks started to make a comeback

themes.theme: BabyLM as the small-data proving ground

insights.claim: BabyLM, an annual competition that grew out of a 2022 Twitter thread between linguist Alex Warstadt and AI researcher Leshem Choshen, now anchors a research community training models on developmentally plausible data budgets.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: Benchmarks define what a field optimizes for; BabyLM is where efficiency-first architectures will show up first.
insights.locator: In August 2022, Warstadt posted a Twitter thread

insights.claim: BabyLM's main track caps training at 100 million words — 10 million for the toddler-scale track — drawn from storybooks, dialogue, movie subtitles, Wikipedia and transcripts of child-directed speech, then scores models on psycholinguistic grammar benchmarks.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: A standardized, cheap evaluation harness lowers the barrier for academic labs to compete on efficiency rather than scale.
insights.quote: a “developmentally plausible” corpus of just 100 million words (for the toddler-scale track, 10 million)
insights.locator: The main event challenges researchers

insights.claim: Models are graded using surprisal — how unlikely a model rates a sentence — against minimal grammatical pairs such as "The keys to the cabinet are on the table" versus the ungrammatical "is" version, mirroring eye-tracking tests run on humans.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: A reusable evaluation model: measure a system's implicit expectations, not just its outputs — applicable well beyond language.
insights.quote: For language models, researchers use a measure called surprisal, which assesses how unlikely the model predicts a sentence or part of a sentence to be.
insights.locator: One kind of task involves presenting test subjects

insights.claim: Curriculum learning — feeding models simple data first and escalating complexity, mimicking baby talk — was the most popular BabyLM approach in round one and underperformed expectations, because transformers apparently do not need ordered data to learn effectively.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: A negative result that saves compute: intuitively appealing data-ordering schemes are not where efficiency gains live.
insights.quote: But it seems like these transformers don’t really need to have their data ordered in such a way to learn effectively.
insights.locator: The competition has already challenged some assumptions

insights.claim: GPT-BERT, the 2024 BabyLM champion, pretrained on about 100 million words and beat Meta's Llama 2 70B — pretrained on roughly 15,000 times more data — on one BabyLM benchmark, by hybridizing next-token prediction with masked-language modeling.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: Proof that architecture and training-objective design can substitute for four orders of magnitude of data on targeted tasks.
insights.quote: when GPT-BERT was pretrained on about 100 million words, it was able to beat the performance of Meta’s Llama 2 70B—an LLM pretrained roughly 15,000 times that amount—on one of the BabyLM benchmarks
insights.locator: Perhaps a touch ironically, the best BabyLM models

insights.claim: The best-performing BabyLM models are not baby-inspired at all, and many small-data models cannot generate text — so benchmark wins on grammar do not translate into usable products.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: Discount headline efficiency claims: narrow benchmark parity is not commercial parity, and the gap is currently large.
insights.quote: Many can’t produce text at all, and even GPT-BERT would seem clunky next to a modern commercial model.
insights.locator: Still, BabyLM models are not on the same level as LLMs

themes.theme: Embodied data: headcams and home recording

insights.claim: SAYCam, built by recruiting three babies of psychologist mothers to wear headcams two hours a week from six months to two and a half years, became the seed corpus that let outside teams train models on genuine child sensory input.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: Data release, not model design, unlocked this subfield — an example of a small open dataset creating an entire research market.
insights.quote: [The families] were willing to release that video, and that’s critical,
insights.locator: So he and four colleagues recruited three babies

insights.claim: Brenden Lake's team trained a model on just 61 hours of raw SAYCam footage that learned to identify objects and map them to words without any of the innate biases developmental theories assumed were required.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: Another prior-free result: mechanisms assumed to need built-in structure keep falling to plain statistical learning.
insights.quote: It turns out you can get a real start on language learning using a lot less than what a number of theories suggested,
insights.locator: But the model Lake’s team built

insights.claim: Lake is explicit that these models still fall far short of childlike capability, cautioning that a two-year-old does not come out the other end of training.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: Keeps expectations calibrated: video grounding is a research direction, not a near-term product path.
insights.quote: we don’t get a two-year-old out of [training] when we’re done.
insights.locator: Still, he adds

insights.claim: Princeton's Uri Hasson spent five years wiring the homes of 17 children with cameras and microphones to record 12 hours a day for the first 1,000 days of life, a dataset only workable because new AI transcription and video-analysis tools exist.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: AI tooling is now unlocking datasets that were previously impossible to process — a compounding loop worth tracking across research fields.
insights.quote: For the first time, we have the input,
insights.locator: Uri Hasson, a neuroscientist and psychologist at Princeton

insights.claim: Adding visual data to text has so far not improved BabyLM entrants, and video-trained multimodal models learn only simple words like "ball" and "cat" — so multimodality is not yet the answer to data efficiency.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: Tempering evidence against the thesis that grounding in video is the near-term unlock for sample efficiency.
insights.quote: Attempts to supplement text with visual data haven’t worked for BabyLM participants, says Warstadt.
insights.locator: So far, training models on video has proved difficult

insights.claim: Headcam studies capture at best a few hours a week, forcing researchers to choose between a thin slice of one child's life or pooled footage from many children — neither of which resembles a child's continuous lived experience.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: Names the structural data-collection limit; whoever solves continuous, consented embodied capture controls the input for this field.
insights.locator: After all, babies can’t wear a headcam 24-7

themes.theme: Active and social learning as the missing ingredient

insights.claim: Gopnik argues children are not passive observers but active experimenters who choose their own data, seeking actions that maximize their "empowerment" — the ability to make a predictable impact on the world.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: An empowerment objective is a concrete alternative training signal to next-token prediction; watch for it in post-transformer architectures.
insights.quote: Children are actively exploring, which means that they’re actively choosing their own data,
insights.locator: Gopnik thinks the issue could be that kids do not simply sit

insights.claim: Harvard's Elizabeth Bonawitz finds children reason about the teacher's knowledge and motives, not just the evidence presented — a pedagogical inference layer that models learning passively and in isolation entirely lack.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: Suggests instruction-tuning that models the intent behind data, rather than the data alone, as an unexploited efficiency lever.
insights.quote: They’re reasoning about the teacher, about the teacher’s knowledge, and about why the teacher is telling [them] this particular information.
insights.locator: Children are not only reasoning about the evidence

insights.claim: BabyLM opened its competition to models that learn by interacting with other models, but the social models did not outperform standard ones — the interaction hypothesis has failed its first empirical test.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: A caution flag for multi-agent training pitches: the nearest published test of the idea came back negative.
insights.quote: But the social models didn’t outperform standard ones.
insights.locator: Last year’s BabyLM actually opened the competition

insights.claim: Unlike models, children know what they don't know and are driven to fill those gaps, pointing to active uncertainty-seeking as a candidate mechanism behind human sample efficiency.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: Maps directly onto active-learning and self-directed data-selection research — a cheaper path than acquiring more data.
insights.quote: Unlike models, children are aware of what they don’t know and have a drive to fill their knowledge gaps
insights.locator: Unlike models, children are aware of what they don’t know

themes.theme: Who is actually funding data efficiency

insights.claim: Among leading industry labs Meta is the most engaged with child-inspired learning: two Meta researchers worked on BabyLM's multimodal branch and Meta scientists recently announced a benchmark and challenge for training models on baby headcam footage.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: Meta is quietly hedging the data-exhaustion risk through academia; a benchmark launch is the cheapest way to source an ecosystem's research output.
insights.quote: Of the leading industry labs, Meta seems the most interested in taking inspiration from kids—specifically for training models from video.
insights.locator: Of the leading industry labs, Meta seems the most interested

insights.claim: A stealth-mode AI startup called Flapping Airplanes has taken an interest in Frank's child-learning research, and neither Meta, Google DeepMind, OpenAI nor Flapping Airplanes agreed to be interviewed about it.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: Universal refusal to comment on a niche academic topic is itself a signal that data-efficiency work is considered competitively sensitive.
insights.quote: Neither Meta, Google DeepMind, OpenAI, nor Flapping Airplanes agreed to an interview.
insights.locator: Frank also says a stealth-mode AI startup

insights.claim: Gopnik predicts frontier labs will not adopt developmental-psychology lessons within the transformer paradigm — it will be whatever architecture replaces the transformer that takes those lessons.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: Timing call: this research is optionality on a post-transformer architecture, not an input to the current product cycle.
insights.quote: She thinks it’ll be the next generation of AI—whatever replaces the transformer—that will take lessons from developmental psychology.
insights.locator: For now, frontier labs aren’t exactly racing

insights.claim: The NanoGPT Slowrun benchmark, launched by Q Labs in March 2026, pursues BabyLM's data-efficiency goal while dropping the human-language-learning motivation entirely — evidence the efficiency agenda is decoupling from cognitive science.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: Data efficiency is becoming a standalone engineering discipline with its own benchmarks — a leading indicator of commercial attention.
insights.quote: But they’ve dropped the motivation from human language learning and really just focused on the data efficiency angle.
insights.locator: An example is the NanoGPT Slowrun benchmark

themes.theme: Strategic stakes: access, minority languages, and models as lab rats

insights.claim: Warstadt's motivation for closing the data gap is competitive access: universities and others without hyperscale resources need efficient training methods to train good models and stay relevant in AI research.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: Efficiency research is the academic sector's route back into frontier-relevant work — expect public funding to follow this framing.
insights.quote: One reason Warstadt wants to close the data gap is to democratize AI so that universities and others without the resources to hyperscale can train good models and stay relevant in AI research.
insights.locator: One reason Warstadt wants to close the data gap

insights.claim: David Samuel of the University of Oslo, a GPT-BERT architect, notes minority languages like Sami may have only tens of millions of tokens available — roughly a toddler's exposure — so small-data techniques are the only route to capable models for those languages.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: Language coverage is a defensible niche: whoever cracks 10^7-token training owns markets English-first labs will not serve.
insights.quote: how can we develop language models that are just as capable as the English ones for small languages?
insights.locator: The question was

insights.claim: Researchers are repurposing language models as a linguistic "model organism" — running experiments like simulating degrees of bilingualism or withholding exposure to grammatical forms that would be impossible to run on real children.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: A second, non-commercial demand curve for cheap trainable models: experimental cognitive science needs many small models, not one large one.
insights.quote: Finally we have a model; not in the sense of a language model, but in the sense of a model organism.
insights.locator: While other animals communicate, only humans converse

insights.claim: Bonawitz, initially skeptical that LLMs could reveal anything about cognition given that brains are embodied, living and continuously changing while LLMs pretrain once and never again, says she is revising her beliefs.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: Notes the one-shot nature of pretraining as a structural difference — continual learning remains the unaddressed architectural gap.
insights.quote: our brains grow and change as we learn and age—LLMs pretrain once and never again
insights.locator: Bonawitz says she was initially skeptical

insights.claim: The lingering scientific ambiguity is whether the data efficiency gap reflects an innate human language instinct or merely better learning algorithms, and models are the first tool capable of adjudicating it.
insights.speaker: Elise Cutts
insights.so_what: If the answer is algorithmic rather than innate, the gap is closable by engineering — the single highest-leverage uncertainty in the story.
insights.quote: Are we born with a language instinct, or would it be possible, even in principle, for a child to learn language purely from experience?
insights.locator: Testing hypotheses about human learning in machine models
